entry.title: Beyond Static Embeddings: Training a 6,000-Parameter RL Agent to Actively Hunt Down Historical Planning Maps

link.title: Beyond Static Embeddings: Training a 6,000-Parameter RL Agent to Actively Hunt Down Historical Planning Maps

entry.content:
Created on October 15, 2026 2026 · reinforcement-learning · markov-decision-processes · computer-vision · sovereign-ai

Why throw a huge LLM or brute-force grid search at a spatial business problem when you can frame it as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and solve it in milliseconds with a tiny policy network in pure NumPy?

Figure 1: Our 6,000-parameter Decision Encoder actively exploring real Ordnance Survey geometry in Trafford. Starting from a rough street-level geocode (blue cross), it zooms out, spots a candidate peak across the neighbourhood, flies over, zooms in to verify, and commits to the exact Land Registry plot (green).

Back in April, I wrote about training a 49-million-parameter contrastive ResNet50 model to geolocate planning documents across Greater Manchester. That approach treated map localization like a giant one-shot classification problem: chop Greater Manchester into 3,478 reference tiles, embed the document, run a matrix multiplication, and hope the nearest tile embedding is the right one.

It worked well as a proof of concept, but as I dug deeper into real-world council archives and started following Sergey Levine’s Deep Reinforcement Learning course (CS285) at UC Berkeley, I realized that one-shot static perception is the wrong abstraction for how real localization works.

When a human caseworker—or an intelligent system—tries to locate a messy, historical planning document on a map, they don’t take a single glance at the entire city and guess. They investigate:

  1. They start at a rough clue (an address, a postcode, or a street name).
  2. They look around at a medium zoom. If the street layout doesn’t match, they zoom out to get their bearings.
  3. If the title block says Scale 1:1250but nothing lines up, they suspect the OCR or title block is wrong and test a 1:2500 scale hypothesis.
  4. In repetitive suburban estates where three cul-de-sacs look almost identical, they jump between rival candidates at fine resolution to compare them side by side.
  5. Most importantly, if the scan is too degraded or ambiguous, they know when to escalate to a human rather than corrupting the database with a bad guess.

Instead of jumping on the LLM wrapper bandwagon, I wanted to see if we could turn this exact operational workflow into a Markov Decision Process (MDP) and train a tiny neural network via Imitation Learning + Reinforcement Learning (REINFORCE) to actively explore the map.

Step 1: Framing Business Economics as an MDP

In reinforcement learning, an agent interacts with an environment over discrete time steps: observing a state $s_t$, picking an action $a_t$ from a menu, and receiving a reward $r_t$.

To test this properly without relying on clean synthetic grids, I built an environment on top of real Ordnance Survey OpenMap Local buildings, Open Roads, and HM Land Registry INSPIRE title polygons across Trafford and Greater Manchester.

The Harder Reality: Hand-Drawn Scans & Demolished Buildings

Lets be honest modern digital plans are easy. The real headache for councils is historical plans they are documents traced by hand decades ago against older maps, where terraced houses were merged into single blocks, pen lines wobble, and 10% to 30% of the buildings on the map have since been demolished or newly built.

On top of visual degradation, the starting address prior is often unreliable:

  • UPRN (45%): Near the property, though 12% of the time it geocodes to the wrong house up to 200m away.
  • Postcode (25%): Anywhere within a 100m to 350m radius of the site.
  • Street (15%): Dropped at a random midpoint along the named road.
  • None (15%): Dropped at a completely random coordinate in a 2.4km $ imes$ 2.4km town.

The Action Space (17 Discrete Decisions)

At each step (up to a budget of 16 looks), the agent views a local crop of the map through a fast Normalized Cross-Correlation (NCC) template matcher and chooses from 17 actions:

  • Navigate: pan_N, pan_E, pan_S, pan_W, zoom_in, zoom_out (switching between 960m coarse, 480m medium, and 240m fine viewports), or goto_peak (center on the highest correlation peak in the current view).
  • Investigate Rivals: The environment keeps a short-term memory of the top 3 distinct match locations seen so far. Picking check_0, check_1, or check_2 jumps straight to that candidate at the finest zoom level to verify it.
  • Gather Clues & Test Hypotheses: read_street runs OCR on the plan to unlock street jump candidates (jump_0..2), while switch_scale flips the agent’s scale hypothesis between 1:1250 and 1:2500 (since 25% of plans have misread or missing scale text).
  • Terminal Actions (commit vs. escalate): Committing runs a sub-pixel registration and checks if the plan’s red boundary polygon overlaps the true Land Registry plot ($ ext{IoU} \ge 0.5$). Escalating stops the search and flags the document for human review.

Step 2: The Brain (A 6,000-Parameter Decision Encoder in Pure NumPy)

Does the RL policy need to be a massive Vision Transformer? No.

The template matcher already turns image comparisons into spatial correlation surfaces. What the agent actually needs is a sequential decision policy that looks at the summary statistics of the search so far and decides what to do next.

I built a DecisionEncoder in pure NumPy—a two-layer, 64-unit tanh Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with a companion Value Network baseline:

  • At each step, it takes a 48-dimensional global situation vector $G$ (current zoom, remaining step budget, current peak score, peak distinctiveness over the runner-up, distance from the geocode, scale state, and the score lead of the top remembered candidates) concatenated with a 21-dimensional per-action feature vector $A[a]$.
  • Because it operates on structured state-action features [situation; option], the entire policy network is roughly 6,000 parameters, runs in microseconds on a CPU, and requires zero deep learning frameworks.

Step 3: SFT Then RL (Why RL From Scratch Fails)

To train the policy, I used the two-stage pipeline standard in modern RL:

  1. Supervised Fine-Tuning / Behavior Cloning (SFT): First, I wrote two rule-based heuristic agents (coarse_to_fine and a more cautious smart_expert that double-checks rival peaks) and recorded 2,400 episodes (~20,500 expert decisions) on a 2.4km $ imes$ 2.4km training area in Trafford. The MLP is trained via cross-entropy to imitate the expert (96.8% action accuracy).
  2. REINFORCE with a Learned Value Baseline: Starting from the cloned weights, the agent plays its own rollouts. For every trajectory $ au$, we compute the reward-to-go $R_t = \sum_{t’=t}^{T} r_{t’}$ and subtract the Value Network’s expected return $V_\phi(s_t)$ to get the Advantage:
\[A_t = R_t - V_\phi(s_t)\]

We then update the policy weights along the policy gradient, combined with an entropy bonus $\mathcal{H}(\pi_ heta)$ to encourage exploration and annealed potential-based distance shaping:

\[ abla_ heta J( heta) \approx rac{1}{N} \sum_{i, t} abla_ heta \log \pi_ heta(a_{i,t} \mid s_{i,t}) \cdot A_{i,t} + eta abla_ heta \mathcal{H}(\pi_ heta(\cdot \mid s_{i,t}))\]

The “Always Escalate” Trap When Training RL From Scratch

What happens if you skip Behavior Cloning and train REINFORCE from random weights (--scratch)?

In our experiments, a randomly initialized agent wanders around the map and makes random commits, losing -1.0 eighty percent of the time (for an average starting return of -0.66). Within 50 iterations, RL-from-scratch discovers a clever, degenerate local optimum: if it simply presses escalate on Step 1 of every single episode, it collects a guaranteed -0.35 reward with 0% wrong commits! Once it collapses into 100% instant escalation, it never experiences a +1.0 commit again.

Warm-starting with Behavior Cloning (SFT) places the policy into the region of state space where it actually finds maps, and REINFORCE (SFT+RL) then refines its decision boundaries far beyond the expert it copied.

Figure 2: Step-by-step filmstrip of the SFT+RL agent locating a degraded hand-drawn plan (`hand` style, where buildings have changed since the plan was drawn). Each panel shows the agent's local viewport crop, the matcher peak (orange crosshair), and the Decision Encoder's live action probability distribution._

Results: Evaluating on Unseen Trafford Map Geometry

I trained the system on 1,200 plans in one 2.4km $ imes$ 2.4km area of Trafford (BNG 374000, 393000) and evaluated every method on the exact same 400 unseen test episodes in a separate 2.4km $ imes$ 2.4km town (BNG 377000, 391000).

Method Correct (Recall) Wrong (Bad Commit) Escalate Avg Looks Precision Total Reward
Geocode Commit (no search) 32.8% 17.0% 50.2% 1.0 65.8% -0.018
Exhaustive Grid (1 scale) 29.5% 1.3% 69.3% 26.0 95.9% -0.460
Exhaustive Grid (both scales) 30.0% 1.8% 68.2% 51.0 94.5% -0.956
Coarse-to-Fine (heuristic) 65.7% 5.2% 29.0% 6.7 92.6% +0.355
Smart Expert (heuristic) 58.5% 2.5% 39.0% 8.3 95.9% +0.267
Pure SFT (Behavior Cloning) 59.0% 2.5% 38.5% 8.2 95.9% +0.265
SFT + RL (REINFORCE) 76.2% 7.0% 16.8% 5.2 91.6% +0.548

Paired 95% bootstrap confidence interval of SFT + RL over the best hand-written baseline (coarse_to_fine): **Reward +0.193 [+0.126, +0.254]**, **Correct +10.5% [+6.5%, +14.2%]**, while taking **1.5 fewer looks** per plan.

Where RL Crushes Rules: Hand-Drawn & Historical Plans (hand style)

When we break down the results by plan style and starting address quality, we see why learned sequential policies beat hand-tuned thresholds:

Subset Coarse-to-Fine Smart Expert Pure SFT (Cloned) SFT + RL (Ours)
Hand-Drawn + Demolished Buildings (hand) 66% (7.0 steps) 60% (8.4 steps) 56% (8.8 steps) 78% (5.3 steps, 92% prec)
Modern Colour (os_colour) 65% (6.6 steps) 55% (8.6 steps) 59% (8.0 steps) 78% (4.9 steps, 89% prec)
Modern Monochrome (os_mono) 66% (6.6 steps) 60% (8.1 steps) 60% (7.9 steps) 75% (5.3 steps, 92% prec)
Exact / Near Address (uprn) 81% (4.6 steps) 70% (6.4 steps) 70% (6.3 steps) 91% (3.1 steps, 94% prec)
Postcode Only (100–350m off) 64% (7.0 steps) 55% (8.8 steps) 57% (8.4 steps) 83% (5.5 steps, 91% prec)
Standard 1:1250 Plans 71% (6.2 steps) 65% (7.5 steps) 66% (7.4 steps) 81% (5.0 steps, 96% prec)

Look at what happened between Pure SFT (59.0% overall, 56% on hand-drawn) and SFT + RL (76.2% overall, 78% on hand-drawn):

  • The hand-written smart_expert was tuned to be cautious (95.9% precision), which caused it to second-guess itself on degraded hand-drawn plans—burning 8.4 steps checking rival peaks and escalating 40% of the time.
  • Pure Behavior Cloning (sft_decision_encoder) faithfully copied that hesitation (56% correct in 8.8 steps).
  • Once unleashed with REINFORCE, the policy discovered that it didn’t need a rigid correlation threshold. By combining the current peak score, local distinctiveness (score - second), and the lead over remembered candidates in obs(), SFT + RL boosted recall on hand-drawn historical plans by +22% over the cloned expert (56% $ ightarrow$ 78%) while cutting search time from 8.8 steps down to 5.3 steps!

The Takeaway: Small MDPs Over Giant Models

There is a temptation in AI engineering right now to treat every multi-step business problem as a prompt-engineering exercise for a massive vision-language model.

But when you strip a problem down to its actual structure—what is the state, what are the actions, and what are the business costs of time, errors, and human escalation—you can often solve it with a 6,000-parameter network that trains on a laptop CPU in 15 minutes and executes in microseconds.

By pairing fast classical signal processing (Normalized Cross-Correlation) with a lightweight RL decision policy (SFT + REINFORCE), our agent doesn’t just recognize maps—it actively hunts them down, adapts to hand-drawn historical drift, verifies its own hypotheses, and knows when to ask a human for help.

entry.title: Sovereign AI for Greater Manchester: Geolocating 20 Years of Planning Docs with Edge-Ready Models

link.title: Sovereign AI for Greater Manchester: Geolocating 20 Years of Planning Docs with Edge-Ready Models

entry.content:
Training a single 49-million-parameter model to match planning documents to Ordnance Survey Maps for the entirety of Greater Manchester!

🚀 Live Interactive Demo

I have deployed the model to a public Hugging Face Space. You can test the 3,478-tile scale test in real-time here:
Greater Manchester Map Matcher Live Dashboard

Most plans within the past 20 years rely on data taken from Ordnance Survey (OS) mapping. Before this, people used to hand-draw buildings, roads, and trees with pencils and pens—hatching lines, hand-signing certain sections, and smudging ink. The great thing with ‘new’ mapping is that people generally no longer go through this effort and use these official tiles instead.

This does raise an interesting question: can we train a system on these actual maps for the purpose of being able to place plans exactly where they belong on an official map? Any such system would need to match the visual patterns of roads, buildings, and rivers as a form of spatial fingerprinting. It feels like this is something that should be possible with relatively small compute, without the need to rely on huge multi-billion parameter models and squashing their capabilities into this quite niche task.

Richard Sutton’s “The Bitter Lesson” comes to mind here; a lot of advanced prompting strategies and “agent” frameworks that many AI Engineers put together are trying to encode complexity into a process which should just be a job for deep learning to learn by itself.

First thing I like to think about when starting any AI project (and this one is no different), where is the data going to come from to prove this out? One exciting area is the possibility of synthesising new forms of data for the purposes of training intelligent systems that generalise. Inspired by early DeepMind experiments such as AlphaGo (which learned through self-play) and their work on Atari games combined with reinforcement learning, I thought it would be interesting to gamify the process of matching planning documents back to their OS Map location. The plans should reflect what we would see in actual council plans, which might be poor scans or have distractors such as stamps and large white spaces on the page.

If I could train a model to recognize spatial fingerprints associated with roads, rivers, and buildings, it should be able to locate a planning document simply by looking at the map. This would mean no text reading, no ground control points, and no complex georeferencing transforms. Just visual pattern matching which is a field where deep learning models have excelled since the “AlexNet moment” way back in 2012.

Step 1: Building the Environment

I started with OS Open Map Local data, which is free vector data covering all of Great Britain, including roads, buildings, water, woodland, and railways. Using this, I rendered a grid of clean reference tiles covering Greater Manchester: 3,478 tiles, each representing a 1km × 1km area. Each tile captures the raw spatial structure of its location: road layout, building footprints, and water features.

I built a synthetic document generator that produces realistic planning documents from the OS vector data. Each document includes:

  • The map rendered in color or monochrome OS styles.
  • Title blocks (“HM Land Registry”, “Planning Application”, council names).
  • Scale bars, north arrows, copyright notices.
  • Road name labels at appropriate angles.
  • Building numbers.
  • Subject property highlighting with red outlines and hatching.
  • Randomized page layouts (portrait/landscape, varying margins).
Figure 1: Examples of synthetic planning documents generated with perfect ground truth.

The key point, though, is that I know exactly where each document is located, giving me perfect ground truth for training!

Step 2: Contrastive Learning

The model architecture is conceptually simple: a dual encoder trained with contrastive loss, similar to CLIP but for maps. Two ResNet50 encoders (pretrained on ImageNet) map images into a shared 256-dimensional embedding space:

  1. The query encoder processes planning documents.
  2. The tile encoder processes reference map tiles.

During training, matching pairs (a planning document and its corresponding tile) are pushed together in embedding space, while non-matching pairs are pushed apart. The model learns to ignore rendering styles, title blocks, labels, and annotations, focusing instead on the spatial features that identify a location.

I utilized ResNet50 as it meant I did not have to go through the pain and effort of teaching the model to recognize shapes and patterns from scratch. At inference time, encoding a new planning document and finding the nearest tile embedding is a single matrix multiplication so essentially instant. All my results and training have been conducted on a single MacBook Pro.

Results: Urmston (Proof of Concept)

On a 4km × 4km area with 225 tiles:

Metric Value
Top-1 Accuracy 65%
Top-5 Accuracy 98.6%
Random Chance 0.4%
Parameters 49M (ResNet50 backbone)
Training Time ~50 minutes on a MacBook Pro

The correct tile is in the model’s top 5 guesses 98.6% of the time.

Results: Greater Manchester (Scale Test)

Scaling to all of Greater Manchester—3,478 tiles covering a 30km × 30km area—with only 1,993 training documents (less than one per tile on average):

Metric Value
Top-1 Accuracy 51.4%
Top-5 Accuracy 79.8%
Random Chance 0.03%
Training Documents 1,993
Total Tiles 3,478
Figure 2: The model identifying correct tiles across a major metropolitan area.

The model correctly identifies the exact 1km square more than half the time, and the correct location is in the top 5 guesses four-fifths of the time across a major metropolitan area. This is achieved with completely different rendering styles between the planning documents and reference tiles.

For context, this is achieved with less than one training example per tile. The model is genuinely learning spatial features, not memorizing. Its learning to ignore the noise contained in planning documents and focus on the map portion of the page for visual clues.

Figure 3: The model identifying correct tiles across a major metropolitan area.

The Takeaway

The big takeaway here is the synthetic data pipeline. The ability to generate unlimited, perfectly-labeled planning documents from OS vector data is a powerful idea. The approach is simple enough that a single developer can build it on a laptop, and the pipeline can be retrained for any council area using freely available OS data.

For councils with backlogs of modern planning documents, a tool that takes a scanned plan and says “this is located here” could be built, trained, and deployed locally for effectively zero cost. No API subscriptions, no cloud dependencies, and no per-document charges.

As the model is a lean 49 million parameters, it doesn’t require a high-end GPU for deployment either. In fact, the entire inference engine and the database of Manchester’s spatial fingerprints could run on a Raspberry Pi. This makes ‘Sovereign AI’ a reality for local government: high-performance geolocation that is offline, private, and runs on cheap & small hardware.

entry.title: Building a GAIA-1 Style World Model for Indoor Robot Navigation

link.title: Building a GAIA-1 Style World Model for Indoor Robot Navigation

entry.content:
What is a World Model?

A world model is a neural network that learns to predict what the world will look like next given a current observation and an action. Instead of directly learning a policy (what action to take), you first learn the dynamics of the environment and then you can plan, imagine counterfactuals, and reason about consequences.

This is the core idea behind GAIA-1 from Wayve, which does this for autonomous driving at scale. I wanted to build something similar for indoor robot navigation. Wayve as a company I think we should be really proud of in the UK, originally starting in Cambridge they are now leading the way with autonomous vehicles and their cars are on our roads in the UK today. Home robotics is an area ripe with research and investment and is one area we are seeing huge advancements.

The best way to achieve my aim here and learn, as always, is to get hands on and try and solve a problem after all “What I cannot create, I do not understand” - Feynman.

The Setup

First things first I set about buying and building a raspberry PI controlled car. This would work as my data collection engine and through tele-operation, I would collect information about my home. It collects data in RGB frames at ~10fps paired with motor commands (left/right wheel speeds). Each trajectory is a few hundred frames of the robot navigating through rooms.

Did some tinkering and got the rig together, I then was able to SSH into the car and upload some .py files for it to take commands and send visuals from its camera back using pyzmq.

Figure 1: PI car after finishing the build.

The pipeline has two stages:

Stage 1 — DINO VQ-VAE: Compress each 128×128 image frame into 64 discrete tokens using a Vector Quantised VAE with a DINO distillation loss. This gives semantically meaningful tokens — similar scene regions get similar token IDs. These tokens become useful as my Transformer that I want to train can use these tokens as a representation of say a couch or a rug as a means to view how it changes with the respective robot actions. We know through GPT models how powerful these models can use language tokens to help users and perform coding tasks etc. Instead of just minimizing pixel-wise error (which leads to blurry averages), the DINO distillation forces the VQ-VAE to group pixels into semantic clusters. It learns that a ‘rug’ is a single entity, making the Transformer’s job of moving the rug with actions much easier.

Stage 2 — GAIA Transformer: A causal GPT-style transformer trained on sequences of [frame_tokens, action, frame_tokens, action, ...]. Given N context frames and an action, it predicts the next frame’s tokens autoregressively. The transformer here is trained on the trajectories of these compressed latent representations of my home and learns how to recreate these latents frame by frame so when I feed the latent back into the decoder portion of my above mentioned VQ-VAE it should be able to build the images back up!

You could say I am creating a mini ‘world’ model of my own home here….we have Wayve at home!

Figure 2: Rollout trajectories examples, notice the rugs and cabinets changing with turns.

Results

The model learned real spatial structure from trajectory data alone there is no 3D supervision, no depth sensors. Applying TURN_LEFT causes the scene to pan right; applying TURN_RIGHT enough steps eventually reveals a completely different part of the room.

Most impressively, the model maintains “object permanence.” If it pans away from the couch and then turns back, the couch reappears in the correct relative position. It has internalized the room’s geometry.

Below is model generated.

Figure 3: Imagined rollout. The model "dreams" a 360-degree turn based on consecutive actions.

What’s Next

  • Better action conditioning (continuous motor values instead of 5 discrete actions)
  • Longer rollouts with less drift
  • Using the world model for planning and policy learning
entry.summary: How I trained an action-conditioned video world model from scratch on a home robot dataset.
